claim: Using SNP array data from 98 meioses, 103 sites affected by NCO were identified.
source: Using SNP array data from 98 meioses, we identified 103 sites affected by NCO, of which 50/52 were confirmed in sequence data.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of NCO sites identified from SNP array data analysis.

claim: 50 out of 52 NCO sites with available sequence data were confirmed in sequence data.
source: Using SNP array data from 98 meioses, we identified 103 sites affected by NCO, of which 50/52 were confirmed in sequence data.
evidence: The manuscript reports validation results from sequence data.

claim: Most NCO events are likely of meiotic origin based on overlap with double strand break (DSB) hotspots.
source: Overlap with double strand break (DSB) hotspots indicates that most of the events are likely of meiotic origin.
evidence: The manuscript infers meiotic origin from overlap analysis with DSB hotspots.

claim: A site is involved in a NCO at a rate of 5.9 × 10−6/bp/generation.
source: We estimate that a site is involved in a NCO at a rate of 5.9 × 10−6/bp/generation, consistent with sperm-typing studies, and infer that tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude.
evidence: The manuscript reports a calculated rate from the data analysis.

claim: The estimated NCO rate is consistent with sperm-typing studies.
source: We estimate that a site is involved in a NCO at a rate of 5.9 × 10−6/bp/generation, consistent with sperm-typing studies, and infer that tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude.
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to previous sperm-typing studies.

claim: NCO tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude.
source: We estimate that a site is involved in a NCO at a rate of 5.9 × 10−6/bp/generation, consistent with sperm-typing studies, and infer that tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude.
evidence: The manuscript infers tract length variation from the data.

claim: Observed NCO events show strong allelic bias at heterozygous AT/GC SNPs, with 68% (58–78%) transmitting GC alleles (p = 5 × 10−4).
source: Observed NCO events show strong allelic bias at heterozygous AT/GC SNPs, with 68% (58–78%) transmitting GC alleles (p = 5 × 10−4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of allelic transmission bias.

claim: In 4 of 15 regions with resequencing data, multiple disjoint NCO tracts cluster in close proximity (∼20–30 kb).
source: Strikingly, in 4 of 15 regions with resequencing data, multiple disjoint NCO tracts cluster in close proximity (∼20–30 kb), a phenomenon not previously seen in mammals.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from resequencing data analysis.

claim: Clustered disjoint NCO tracts is a phenomenon not previously seen in mammals.
source: Strikingly, in 4 of 15 regions with resequencing data, multiple disjoint NCO tracts cluster in close proximity (∼20–30 kb), a phenomenon not previously seen in mammals.
evidence: The manuscript states this is a novel observation in mammals.

claim: Meiotic recombination deliberately inflicts double strand breaks (DSBs) on the genome.
source: Meiotic recombination is a process that deliberately inflicts double strand breaks (DSBs) on the genome, leading to their repair as either crossover (CO) or non-crossover (NCO) resolutions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiotic recombination.

claim: DSBs are repaired as either crossover (CO) or non-crossover (NCO) resolutions.
source: Meiotic recombination is a process that deliberately inflicts double strand breaks (DSBs) on the genome, leading to their repair as either crossover (CO) or non-crossover (NCO) resolutions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DSB repair outcomes.

claim: COs play an essential role in the segregation of chromosomes during meiosis.
source: COs play an essential role in the segregation of chromosomes during meiosis whereas NCOs are thought to aid in homolog pairing or in shaping the distribution of COs over the genome (Cole et al., 2012b; Baudat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: NCOs are thought to aid in homolog pairing or in shaping the distribution of COs over the genome.
source: COs play an essential role in the segregation of chromosomes during meiosis whereas NCOs are thought to aid in homolog pairing or in shaping the distribution of COs over the genome (Cole et al., 2012b; Baudat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous studies.

claim: The past decade has seen tremendous progress in characterization of DSBs and COs in mammals.
source: While the past decade has seen tremendous progress in our characterization of DSBs and COs in mammals (Baudat et al., 2013), little is known about NCO events.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by citation.

claim: Little is known about NCO events.
source: While the past decade has seen tremendous progress in our characterization of DSBs and COs in mammals (Baudat et al., 2013), little is known about NCO events.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: CO and NCO resolutions appear to result from a choice early on in the repair of DSB breaks.
source: These two resolutions appear to result from a choice early on in the repair of DSB breaks (Youds and Boulton, 2011), with a number of properties differing between them (Cole et al., 2012b, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Both CO and NCO outcomes are accompanied by a short gene conversion tract.
source: In particular, both outcomes are accompanied by a short gene conversion tract that fills in the DSB on one homologous chromosome with the sequence from the other homolog.
evidence: This is established knowledge about recombination outcomes.

claim: COs yield chromosomes with multi-megabase long segments from each homolog.
source: Whereas COs yield chromosomes with multi-megabase long segments from each homolog (Baudat et al., 2013), NCO gene conversion tracts have been estimated to span ∼50–1000 bp (Jeffreys and May, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: NCO gene conversion tracts have been estimated to span ∼50–1000 bp.
source: Whereas COs yield chromosomes with multi-megabase long segments from each homolog (Baudat et al., 2013), NCO gene conversion tracts have been estimated to span ∼50–1000 bp (Jeffreys and May, 2004).
evidence: This is an estimate from a previous study.

claim: NCO gene conversion tracts affect sequence variation by breaking down linkage disequilibrium (LD) within a localized region.
source: Although short, these NCO gene conversion tracts affect sequence variation by breaking down linkage disequilibrium (LD) within a localized region, and, together with COs, are necessary to explain present-day haplotype diversity (Przeworski and Wall, 2001; Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of NCO.

claim: NCO gene conversion tracts, together with COs, are necessary to explain present-day haplotype diversity.
source: Although short, these NCO gene conversion tracts affect sequence variation by breaking down linkage disequilibrium (LD) within a localized region, and, together with COs, are necessary to explain present-day haplotype diversity (Przeworski and Wall, 2001; Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: The frequency with which NCOs occur in mammals remains uncharacterized.
source: Despite the importance of NCOs, the frequency with which they occur in mammals remains uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Estimates based on the number of DSBs that occur in meiosis suggest that NCOs are an order of magnitude more frequent than COs.
source: Estimates based on the number of DSBs that occur in meiosis suggest that NCOs are an order of magnitude more frequent than COs (Baudat and de Massy, 2007; Cole et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is an estimate from previous studies.

claim: Sperm-typing studies and analyses of LD indicate that NCOs occur ∼1 to 15 fold more frequently than COs.
source: In turn, sperm-typing studies and analyses of LD indicate that NCOs occur ∼1 to 15 fold more frequently than COs (Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001; Jeffreys and May, 2004; Gay et al., 2007; Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014), with this value varying widely in analyses of individual hotspots (Jeffreys and May, 2004; Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies.

claim: The NCO to CO ratio varies widely in analyses of individual hotspots.
source: In turn, sperm-typing studies and analyses of LD indicate that NCOs occur ∼1 to 15 fold more frequently than COs (Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001; Jeffreys and May, 2004; Gay et al., 2007; Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014), with this value varying widely in analyses of individual hotspots (Jeffreys and May, 2004; Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies.

claim: COs occur at a higher rate in females than in males.
source: Furthermore, while COs occur at a higher rate in females than in males and tend to occur in different genomic locations between the sexes (Kong et al., 2010), there has been no such comparison for NCO events.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: COs tend to occur in different genomic locations between the sexes.
source: Furthermore, while COs occur at a higher rate in females than in males and tend to occur in different genomic locations between the sexes (Kong et al., 2010), there has been no such comparison for NCO events.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: There has been no comparison of NCO rates or locations between sexes.
source: Furthermore, while COs occur at a higher rate in females than in males and tend to occur in different genomic locations between the sexes (Kong et al., 2010), there has been no such comparison for NCO events.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: NCO events are assumed to occur at the same hotspots for DSBs as COs.
source: While NCO events are assumed to occur at the same hotspots for DSBs as COs (Baudat et al., 2013), in humans, this has only been demonstrated for a limited number of locations in sperm (Berg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a general assumption in the field cited from previous studies.

claim: In humans, NCO events occurring at the same hotspots as COs has only been demonstrated for a limited number of locations in sperm.
source: While NCO events are assumed to occur at the same hotspots for DSBs as COs (Baudat et al., 2013), in humans, this has only been demonstrated for a limited number of locations in sperm (Berg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the limited evidence from previous studies.

claim: Sperm-typing studies have identified complex COs in which gene conversion tracts occur near but not contiguous with CO breakpoints.
source: Furthermore, by considering events in a single meiosis, sperm-typing studies have identified complex COs in which gene conversions tracts occur near but not contiguous with CO breakpoints (Webb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: In highly recombining regions, GC content increases over evolutionary time.
source: Cross-species analyses have shown that in highly recombining regions, GC content increases over evolutionary time, consistent with an important role for GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-species analyses cited from a previous study.

claim: The increase in GC content in highly recombining regions is consistent with an important role for GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC).
source: Cross-species analyses have shown that in highly recombining regions, GC content increases over evolutionary time, consistent with an important role for GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of cross-species data cited from a previous study.

claim: Polymorphism data reveal an effect of recombination, with more AT to GC polymorphisms observed in regions of higher recombination.
source: Polymorphism data also reveal an effect of recombination, with more AT to GC polymorphisms observed in regions of higher recombination (Auton et al., 2012; Pratto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from polymorphism data cited from previous studies.

claim: gBGC acts analogously to positive selection.
source: Moreover, because gBGC acts analogously to positive selection, its effects on polymorphism and divergence can confound studies of human adaptation (Galtier and Duret, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: The effects of gBGC on polymorphism and divergence can confound studies of human adaptation.
source: Moreover, because gBGC acts analogously to positive selection, its effects on polymorphism and divergence can confound studies of human adaptation (Galtier and Duret, 2007).
evidence: This is a consequence of gBGC cited from a previous study.

claim: One recent sperm-typing study reported two recombination hotspots that exhibit GC-bias in NCO resolutions.
source: Although one recent sperm-typing study reported two recombination hotspots that exhibit GC-bias in NCO resolutions (Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014), most of the evidence of gBGC in mammals is indirect.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: Most of the evidence of gBGC in mammals is indirect.
source: Although one recent sperm-typing study reported two recombination hotspots that exhibit GC-bias in NCO resolutions (Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014), most of the evidence of gBGC in mammals is indirect.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of evidence in the field.

claim: This is the first genome-wide assay of de novo NCO gene conversion in mammals.
source: Motivated by these considerations, we carried out a study of NCO gene conversion events in pedigrees—to our knowledge, the first genome-wide assay of de novo NCO gene conversion in mammals.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The primary analysis focused on SNP array data from 34 three-generation pedigrees.
source: The primary analysis focused on SNP array data from 34 three-generation pedigrees.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The SNP array data provide information from 98 meioses, 49 paternal and 49 maternal.
source: These SNP array data provide information from 98 meioses, 49 paternal and 49 maternal, and are informative at 12.1 million sites (markers where we can potentially detect a NCO in a parent-child transmission).
evidence: This describes the study design and data.

claim: The SNP array data are informative at 12.1 million sites.
source: These SNP array data provide information from 98 meioses, 49 paternal and 49 maternal, and are informative at 12.1 million sites (markers where we can potentially detect a NCO in a parent-child transmission).

claim: 97 NCO sites were identified with standard ascertainment.
source: This analysis revealed a total of 103 SNP sites (henceforth 'NCO sites') putatively affected by autosomal NCO events: 97 with standard ascertainment, and an additional six that are detectable but do not meet all the criteria for inclusion in the rate calculation (Figure 1C; Source code 1; 'Materials and methods'—'Determination of informative sites').

claim: An additional six NCO sites are detectable but do not meet all the criteria for inclusion in the rate calculation.
source: This analysis revealed a total of 103 SNP sites (henceforth 'NCO sites') putatively affected by autosomal NCO events: 97 with standard ascertainment, and an additional six that are detectable but do not meet all the criteria for inclusion in the rate calculation (Figure 1C; Source code 1; 'Materials and methods'—'Determination of informative sites').

source: Most (76/103) NCO events derive from a single SNP, while others contain two or three NCO sites that delimit a tract.

source: Most (76/103) NCO events derive from a single SNP, while others contain two or three NCO sites that delimit a tract.

source: The NCO sites have roughly equal numbers of homozygous and heterozygous genotype calls in the recipient (53% heterozygous sites, p = 0.56, two-sided binomial test, this and other statistical analyses included in Source code 2), as expected, providing further confidence that the calls are not spurious.

claim: The roughly equal distribution of homozygous and heterozygous genotype calls in NCO recipients provides further confidence that the calls are not spurious.
source: The NCO sites have roughly equal numbers of homozygous and heterozygous genotype calls in the recipient (53% heterozygous sites, p = 0.56, two-sided binomial test, this and other statistical analyses included in Source code 2), as expected, providing further confidence that the calls are not spurious.

Sequence data were available for 52 of these NCO sites, of which 50 are concordant with the SNP array calls ('Materials and methods'—'Validating NCO events', Source code 1).

claim: For one of the two discordant sites between SNP array and sequence data, the source of error is unclear.

claim: 4.2% of informative sites have CO rate ≥10 cM/Mb.
source: Indeed, 18 of the 72 events that we can examine (26%) localize to such regions (using only one SNP per NCO event), while 4.2% of informative sites have this high a rate.

source: This co-localization is unlikely to occur by chance (p = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided binomial test), indicating that NCOs are strongly enriched in CO hotspots, and providing further validation that the detected NCO events are real.

claim: NCOs are strongly enriched in CO hotspots.
source: This co-localization is unlikely to occur by chance (p = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided binomial test), indicating that NCOs are strongly enriched in CO hotspots, and providing further validation that the detected NCO events are real.

source: The enrichment of NCO in regions with high rates of meiotic CO suggests that the NCO resolutions are meiotic in origin.

claim: Only 5.5% of informative sites overlap a DSB hotspot.

claim: NCO events tend to occur at sites of meiotic DSB.
source: Thus, the NCOs tend to occur at sites of meiotic DSB.

claim: 56% (15/27) of NCO events in male PRDM9 A/B-only carriers overlap LD-based hotspots.
source: Considering all unambiguous NCO event locations in male PRDM9 A/B-only carriers, 56% (15/27) overlap the (population-averaged) LD-based hotspots (The International HapMap Consortium, 2007), when between 52% and 63% of DSB hotspots from spermatocytes do, depending on the source population of the LD map analyzed (Pratto et al., 2014).
evidence: This reports the overlap between NCO events and LD-based hotspots.

claim: Between 52% and 63% of DSB hotspots from spermatocytes overlap LD-based hotspots, depending on the source population of the LD map analyzed.
source: Considering all unambiguous NCO event locations in male PRDM9 A/B-only carriers, 56% (15/27) overlap the (population-averaged) LD-based hotspots (The International HapMap Consortium, 2007), when between 52% and 63% of DSB hotspots from spermatocytes do, depending on the source population of the LD map analyzed (Pratto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: The rate at which NCO events overlap LD-based hotspots is almost identical to the rate at which meiotic DSBs occur in such locations.

source: The overlap for NCO events from both sexes is similar, with 55% (28/51) of events overlapping LD-based hotspots.

claim: Fragile sites are one of the important sources of mitotic recombination.

claim: The SNP array data are enriched for regions of high recombination relative to the full genome.
source: As Figure 2A shows, however, our SNP array data are enriched for regions of high recombination relative to the full genome, and it is necessary to account for this bias.

claim: A study by Jeffreys and May examined three hotspots in detail and found the number of NCO events to be 4–15 times that of COs, with a mean tract length of 55–290 bp.

evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: The NCO rate results are concordant with those from sperm-based analyses.
source: Our results are therefore concordant with those from sperm-based analyses; they are also consistent with several LD-based studies of genome-wide levels of NCO (Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001; Gay et al., 2007).

claim: The NCO rate results are consistent with several LD-based studies of genome-wide levels of NCO.
source: Our results are therefore concordant with those from sperm-based analyses; they are also consistent with several LD-based studies of genome-wide levels of NCO (Ardlie et al., 2001; Frisse et al., 2001; Gay et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies.

claim: The two SNP arrays differ significantly in number of events detected per sex (p = 5.1 × 10−4, χ2 one degree of freedom test).
source: Considering the parent of origin of each NCO event, we found that the two SNP arrays differ significantly in number of events detected per sex (p = 5.1 × 10−4, χ2 one degree of freedom [df] test), with the lower density SNP dataset uncovering fewer male-specific events than expected.

claim: The lower density SNP dataset uncovered fewer male-specific events than expected.
source: Considering the parent of origin of each NCO event, we found that the two SNP arrays differ significantly in number of events detected per sex (p = 5.1 × 10−4, χ2 one degree of freedom [df] test), with the lower density SNP dataset uncovering fewer male-specific events than expected.

claim: The bias in male event detection may be caused by a lower coverage of the telomeres in the low density SNP array.

claim: Male NCO events are more prevalent in the telomeres.
source: Nevertheless, considering the position of events captured by genotype arrays reveals broad-scale localization differences, with male events more prevalent in the telomeres and female events relatively dispersed throughout the genome (Figure 1C,D).

claim: Female NCO events are relatively dispersed throughout the genome.
source: Nevertheless, considering the position of events captured by genotype arrays reveals broad-scale localization differences, with male events more prevalent in the telomeres and female events relatively dispersed throughout the genome (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C,D and stated in the text.

claim: Sex differences in NCO localization are similar to those seen for CO events.
source: These sex differences in localization are similar to those seen for CO events (Kong et al., 2010), as expected from a shared mechanism for the broader-scale (e.g., megabase-level) control of both types of recombination.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings on CO events.

claim: Four NCO events overlap sequences that match at least six of the eight predictive bps in the degenerate 13-mer motif bound by PRDM9.

evidence: This reports an observation from the data.

claim: All four NCO events that overlap PRDM9 motifs transmit GC alleles.
source: Because the PRDM9 motif is GC rich, initiation bias would be expected to predominantly transmit AT alleles, but instead all four of these events transmit GC alleles.
evidence: This reports an observation from the data.

claim: For three of the four NCO events overlapping PRDM9 motifs, sequences that match the PRDM9 motif at seven of eight positions occur at other positions within 2 kb of the NCO site.
source: Notably however, for three of the events, sequences that match the PRDM9 motif at seven of eight positions occur at other positions within 2 kb of the NCO site, and for the fourth, another motif with 6 of 8 matching bps occurs within 2 kb.
evidence: This reports an observation from the data.

claim: The four NCO events overlapping PRDM9 motifs may not be caused by initiation bias.
source: Thus, these four events may not be caused by initiation bias.
evidence: This is an inference from the presence of other PRDM9 motifs nearby.

claim: There is no evidence for a difference in GC transmission rate between the two SNP density datasets (p = 0.18, χ2 1-df test).
source: In the NCO events identified here, we saw no evidence for a difference in GC transmission rate between the two SNP density datasets (p = 0.18, χ2 1-df test), or between males and females (p = 0.79, χ2 1-df test), and so considered the data jointly.
evidence: This reports a statistical test of differences.

claim: There is no evidence for a difference in GC transmission rate between males and females (p = 0.79, χ2 1-df test).
source: In the NCO events identified here, we saw no evidence for a difference in GC transmission rate between the two SNP density datasets (p = 0.18, χ2 1-df test), or between males and females (p = 0.79, χ2 1-df test), and so considered the data jointly.
evidence: This reports a statistical test of differences.

claim: Of 92 NCO sites with AT/GC polymorphisms (excluding PRDM9 motif sites and ambiguous sites), 63 transmit G or C alleles (68%, 95% CI 58–78%; p = 5.1 × 10−4, two-sided binomial test).
source: We observed a strong bias towards the transmission of G or C: of the 92 sites, 63 transmit G or C alleles (68%, 95% CI 58–78%; p = 5.1 × 10−4, two-sided binomial test).
evidence: This reports a statistical analysis of GC transmission bias.

claim: 39 of 92 NCO sites are at CpG dinucleotides.
source: SNP variants at CpG dinucleotides account for 39 of these 92 sites, and these also show GC bias, with 25 CpG sites (64%) transmitting GC alleles, and no evidence of rate difference between transmissions at CpG and non-CpG sites (p = 0.58, χ2 1-df test).
evidence: This reports the number of CpG sites among NCO sites.

claim: 25 of 39 CpG NCO sites (64%) transmit GC alleles.
source: SNP variants at CpG dinucleotides account for 39 of these 92 sites, and these also show GC bias, with 25 CpG sites (64%) transmitting GC alleles, and no evidence of rate difference between transmissions at CpG and non-CpG sites (p = 0.58, χ2 1-df test).
evidence: This reports GC transmission at CpG sites.

claim: There is no evidence of rate difference between transmissions at CpG and non-CpG sites (p = 0.58, χ2 1-df test).
source: SNP variants at CpG dinucleotides account for 39 of these 92 sites, and these also show GC bias, with 25 CpG sites (64%) transmitting GC alleles, and no evidence of rate difference between transmissions at CpG and non-CpG sites (p = 0.58, χ2 1-df test).
evidence: This reports a statistical test of differences.

claim: The sperm-typing study by Odenthal-Hesse et al. found that two of six assayed hotspots exhibited detectable levels of gBGC, transmitting GC alleles in ∼70% of NCO transmissions.
source: By comparison, the sperm-typing study noted above found that two of six assayed hotspots exhibited detectable levels of gBGC, and these two loci transmitted GC alleles in ∼70% of NCO transmissions (Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: GC transmission rates are consistent across recombination rate bins (p = 0.67, χ2 5-df test).
source: Across recombination rate bins, we observed consistent GC transmission rates (p = 0.67, χ2 5-df test Figure 2B).
evidence: This reports a statistical test shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The effects of gBGC will be strongest in high recombination rate regions.
source: Since the strength of gBGC depends on both the degree of bias and the rate of recombination, this finding implies that the effects of gBGC will be strongest in high recombination rate regions, as seen in analyses of polymorphism and divergence (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the consistent GC transmission rates across recombination rate bins.

claim: Twelve regions have NCO tracts that include multiple SNPs.
source: As previously noted, most NCO events involve only one SNP, but a total of twelve regions (ten with information from SNP array data only, and two including information from the sequence data) have tracts that include multiple SNPs (as plotted in Figure 3).
evidence: This reports observations from the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Five NCO events have a lower bound on tract length of at least 1 kb.
source: From these data, we deduced that five of these events have a lower bound on tract length of at least 1 kb while the smallest is at least 94 bp.
evidence: This is deduced from the data on multi-SNP tracts.

claim: The smallest multi-SNP NCO tract is at least 94 bp.
source: From these data, we deduced that five of these events have a lower bound on tract length of at least 1 kb while the smallest is at least 94 bp.
evidence: This is deduced from the data on multi-SNP tracts.

claim: One NCO tract is at most 144 bp.
source: In turn, one tract is at most 144 bp—only slightly longer than the minimum tract involving more than one SNP (≥94 bp)—and four events have tracts that must be shorter than 1400 bp.
evidence: This is deduced from the data on tract boundaries.

claim: Four NCO events have tracts that must be shorter than 1400 bp.
source: In turn, one tract is at most 144 bp—only slightly longer than the minimum tract involving more than one SNP (≥94 bp)—and four events have tracts that must be shorter than 1400 bp.
evidence: This is deduced from the data on tract boundaries.

claim: NCO tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude (i.e., 100–1000 bp).
source: These observations, coupled with the variable length in tracts that occur in the clustered NCO events described below (see Figure 4A), suggest that tract lengths span at least an order of magnitude (i.e., 100–1000 bp).
evidence: This is inferred from the range of observed tract lengths.

claim: Complete Genomics resequencing data were used to examine variants surrounding several of the identified NCO events at closer resolution.
source: We used Complete Genomics resequencing data generated by the T2D-GENES Consortium to examine variants surrounding several of the identified NCO events at closer resolution.
evidence: This describes the methods used.

claim: Sequence data were available for two pedigrees with both parents and three children.
source: In order to confidently phase these regions, we required sequence data for both parents and three children (including the NCO event recipient); such data were available for two pedigrees.
evidence: This describes the available data.

claim: In the two pedigrees with sequence data, there are a total of 15 regions with evidence for a NCO event in the SNP array data.
source: In these pedigrees, there are a total of 15 regions with evidence for a NCO event in the SNP array data.
evidence: This reports the number of regions examined.

claim: Two of the 15 regions with NCO evidence are not included in the sequence data analysis.
source: Two of these regions are not included in this analysis: for one, the sequence data do not contain a genotype call for the site putatively affected by NCO, while in the other, genotype calls do not match the sequence data.
evidence: This explains exclusions from the analysis.

claim: In four cases (haplotypes 10–13), multiple disjoint NCO tracts occur within a short interval of less than 30 kb.
source: In four cases (haplotypes 10–13), multiple disjoint NCO tracts occur within a short interval of less than 30 kb, with the discontinuities evident from informative sites located between the NCO tracts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and stated in the text.

claim: Two of the clustered NCO events (haplotypes 11 and 13) occur near COs.
source: Two of these events (haplotypes 11 and 13) occur near COs, and the transmitted haplotypes do not allow us to determine unambiguously which sites experienced the NCO event.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and stated in the text.

claim: The four cases of clustered NCO occur in a single pedigree, three in the mother, and one in the father.
source: The four cases occur in a single pedigree, three in the mother, and one in the father (haplotype 11).
evidence: This reports the distribution of clustered NCO events.

claim: The clustering of NCO events is highly unexpected, with a probability of observing two independent tracts within the four regions ranging from p = 2.9 × 10−6 to 1.9 × 10−4.
source: Using the LD-based genetic map length of the 100 kb around these four regions, we found that this clustering is highly unexpected, with a probability of observing two independent tracts within the four regions ranging from p = 2.9 × 10−6 to 1.9 × 10−4 (for each region independently; see 'Materials and methods'—'Examination of regions containing clustered NCOs').
evidence: This reports a statistical calculation of clustering significance.

claim: Sanger sequencing was performed on individuals from the three-generation pedigrees in which clustered NCOs occurred.
source: We performed Sanger sequencing on individuals from the three-generation pedigrees in which clustered NCOs occurred.
evidence: This describes validation methods.

claim: The Sanger sequence data are concordant with the genotypes from the whole genome sequence data at every site and in all individuals for which genotypes could be called.
source: The Sanger sequence data are concordant with the genotypes from the whole genome sequence data at every site and in all individuals for which we were able to call genotypes (see 'Materials and methods'—'Examination of regions containing clustered NCOs').
evidence: This reports validation results.

claim: The regions with clustered NCO events show no overlap with segmental duplications.
source: We also examined these regions for overlap with segmental duplications, but found none ('Materials and methods'—'Examination of regions containing clustered NCOs').
evidence: This reports a check for potential artifacts.

claim: All four clustered NCO events appear to comprise true NCOs, but caution is warranted in interpreting two of the four cases.
source: Thus, all four events appear to comprise true NCOs, but caution is warranted in interpreting two of the four cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the validation analyses.

claim: For the two unambiguous clustered NCO events (haplotypes 10 and 12), GC alleles were transmitted at 9 out of 10 heterozygous AT/GC SNPs affected by NCO.
source: Intriguingly, the alleles within the NCO events show strong GC bias: For the two unambiguous events (haplotypes 10 and 12), GC alleles were transmitted at 9 out of 10 heterozygous AT/GC SNPs affected by NCO.
evidence: This reports GC transmission in clustered NCO events.

claim: Considering all sites in haplotypes 10–13 contained within or between the NCO tracts, G or C was transmitted at 32 of 43 (74%) heterozygous AT/GC SNPs.
source: Moreover, considering all sites in haplotypes 10–13 contained within or between the NCO tracts and irrespective of NCO status, G or C was transmitted at 32 of 43 (74%) heterozygous AT/GC SNPs ('Materials and methods'—'Examination of regions containing clustered NCOs').
evidence: This reports GC transmission across clustered NCO regions.

claim: The patchy repair resolutions in the four clustered NCO events may result from a GC biased repair process that operates discontinuously within long stretches of heteroduplex DNA.
source: These findings raise the possibility that the patchy repair resolutions observed in the four events result from a GC biased repair process that operates discontinuously within long stretches of heteroduplex DNA.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The clustered NCO results could be explained by repeated template switching, as has been observed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Alternatively, these results could be explained by repeated template switching, as has been observed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Tsaponina and Haber James, 2014).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation citing a mechanism from yeast.

claim: Three more clustered NCO events and six NCO events near but disjoint from CO resolutions were identified in the array-based data.
source: Further examination of our array-based data revealed additional events: three more clustered NCO events as well as six NCO events near but disjoint from CO resolutions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This reports additional observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Two of the haplotypes showing clustered NCO in array data (numbers 18 and 19) are the same cases that show clustered NCO in sequence data (haplotypes 11 and 13).
source: Two of these haplotypes (numbers 18 and 19) are the same cases that show clustered NCO in sequence data (Figure 4A, haplotypes 11 and 13); all other events were seen in distinct pedigrees.
evidence: This clarifies the relationship between observations in different datasets.

claim: Complex CO resolutions previously described in humans were seen in assays of relatively short intervals of ≤4 kb around CO breakpoints, with an estimated frequency of 0.17%.
source: The complex CO events previously described in humans were seen in assays of relatively short intervals of ≤4 kb around CO breakpoints, and yielded an estimated frequency of 0.17% (Webb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: The results from the current study indicate that complex resolutions also occur farther from the CO breakpoint, so may be more common.
source: The results from the current study indicate that complex resolutions also occur farther from the CO breakpoint, so may be more common.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed complex CO events.

claim: This is the first observation of clustered but discontinuous NCO gene conversion tracts in mammals.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first observation of clustered but discontinuous NCO gene conversion tracts in mammals, although patterns that resemble those shown in Figure 4A have been reported in meiosis (Martini et al., 2011; Globus, 2013) and mitosis (St Charles and Petes, 2013; Yin and Petes, 2013) in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the observation.

claim: Patterns resembling clustered NCO tracts have been reported in meiosis and mitosis in S. cerevisiae.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first observation of clustered but discontinuous NCO gene conversion tracts in mammals, although patterns that resemble those shown in Figure 4A have been reported in meiosis (Martini et al., 2011; Globus, 2013) and mitosis (St Charles and Petes, 2013; Yin and Petes, 2013) in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies in yeast.

claim: Some events classified as complex CO in humans may in fact be complex NCO.
source: We further note that some events classified as complex CO in humans (based on a limited number of markers) may in fact be complex NCO (Webb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation about previous observations.

claim: The observed complex NCOs and distant forms of complex CO point to a property of mammalian recombination that is poorly understood and in need of further characterization.
source: The observed complex NCOs and distant forms of complex CO (Figure 4B, haplotypes 17–22) both point to a property of mammalian recombination that is poorly understood and in need of further characterization.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: Five longer-range recombination events were identified: three continuous tracts, and two that showed a clustering pattern.
source: In addition to the NCO events with tracts that span no more than 5 kb, we identified five longer-range recombination events: three continuous tracts, and two that showed a clustering pattern (see Figure 5).
evidence: This reports observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Each longer-range recombination event occurred in a different pedigree.
source: Each event occurred in a different pedigree; the continuous tract that spans ∼79 kb was transmitted by a male, and the four other events occurred in females.
evidence: This reports the distribution of longer-range events.

claim: The continuous tract that spans ∼79 kb was transmitted by a male.
source: Each event occurred in a different pedigree; the continuous tract that spans ∼79 kb was transmitted by a male, and the four other events occurred in females.
evidence: This reports the sex of the transmitter.

claim: Four of the five longer-range recombination events occurred in females.
source: Each event occurred in a different pedigree; the continuous tract that spans ∼79 kb was transmitted by a male, and the four other events occurred in females.
evidence: This reports the sex of the transmitters.

claim: The long continuous tracts could conceivably reflect double COs in extremely close proximity, as might arise from a CO-interference independent pathway.
source: The long continuous tracts could conceivably reflect double COs in extremely close proximity, as might arise from a CO-interference independent pathway (Fledel-Alon et al., 2009), but the clustered events cannot be explained in this way.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The clustered longer-range events cannot be explained by double COs in close proximity.
source: The long continuous tracts could conceivably reflect double COs in extremely close proximity, as might arise from a CO-interference independent pathway (Fledel-Alon et al., 2009), but the clustered events cannot be explained in this way.
evidence: This is an inference from the nature of the clustered events.

claim: For two longer-range events, sequence data are available and validate the genotype calls.
source: For two events, sequence data are available and validate the genotype calls, indicating that the case that spans at least 9 kb in the genotype data is in fact at least 18 kb long (haplotype 23), and confirming the case in which clustered events span ∼203 kb (haplotype 26).
evidence: This reports validation results.

claim: The case that spans at least 9 kb in the genotype data is in fact at least 18 kb long (haplotype 23).
source: For two events, sequence data are available and validate the genotype calls, indicating that the case that spans at least 9 kb in the genotype data is in fact at least 18 kb long (haplotype 23), and confirming the case in which clustered events span ∼203 kb (haplotype 26).
evidence: This reports a finding from sequence data validation.

claim: Haplotypes 23, 24, and 27 reside on the p arm of chromosome 8 where a long inversion polymorphism occurs.
source: Haplotypes 23, 24, and 27 reside on the p arm of chromosome 8 where a long inversion polymorphism occurs (Antonacci et al., 2009).
evidence: This reports the genomic location and context.

claim: The three recombination events on chromosome 8p are >1.7 Mb outside the inversion breakpoints.
source: Single COs within inversion heterozygotes can be misinterpreted as more than one CO event (Broman et al., 2003), yet these three recombination events are >1.7 Mb outside the inversion breakpoints, so should not be affected.
evidence: This reports the distance from the inversion.

claim: The large inversion polymorphism may lead to aberrant synapsis during meiosis, leading to complex repair of DSBs.
source: One possibility is that the large inversion polymorphism leads to aberrant synapsis during meiosis, leading to complex repair of DSBs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The transmitter of haplotype 23 is heterozygous for tag SNPs for the 8p23 inversion polymorphism.
source: In that regard, we note the transmitter of haplotype 23 is heterozygous for tag SNPs for the 8p23 inversion polymorphism (Antonacci et al., 2009), and that a sibling inherited a haplotype from the same parent with a CO at the same position as the end of the tract for haplotype 23.
evidence: This reports a genotype observation.

claim: A sibling of the haplotype 23 recipient inherited a haplotype from the same parent with a CO at the same position as the end of the tract for haplotype 23.
source: In that regard, we note the transmitter of haplotype 23 is heterozygous for tag SNPs for the 8p23 inversion polymorphism (Antonacci et al., 2009), and that a sibling inherited a haplotype from the same parent with a CO at the same position as the end of the tract for haplotype 23.
evidence: This reports an observation about recombination in a sibling.

claim: The co-localization of recombination events in haplotype 23 and a sibling may be due to effects of the inversion on synapsis.
source: This co-localization may be due to effects of the inversion on synapsis; alternatively, this could indicate that the sites are incorrectly positioned, resulting in inaccurate inference of breakpoint locations (Broman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The co-localization of recombination events in haplotype 23 and a sibling could indicate that the sites are incorrectly positioned, resulting in inaccurate inference of breakpoint locations.
source: This co-localization may be due to effects of the inversion on synapsis; alternatively, this could indicate that the sites are incorrectly positioned, resulting in inaccurate inference of breakpoint locations (Broman et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation.

claim: NCO gene conversion reshuffles haplotypes and shapes LD patterns.
source: NCO gene conversion reshuffles haplotypes and shapes LD patterns, at a rate that we estimate to be 5.9 × 10−6/bp/generation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of NCO.

claim: Roughly 17,110 (95% CI 13,340–21,460) sites will be affected by NCO in each generation.
source: This suggests that roughly 17,110 (95% CI 13,340–21,460) sites will be affected by NCO in each generation (for a euchromatic genome length of 2.9 × 109 bp).
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated NCO rate.

claim: If the average tract length were 75 bp, ∼228 NCO events (95% CI 178–286) are expected to occur in each generation.
source: If the average tract length were 75 bp (consistent with Jeffreys and May, 2004; Cole et al., 2014), ∼228 NCO events (95% CI 178–286) are expected to occur in each generation.
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated NCO rate and an assumed tract length.

claim: The sex-averaged number of COs is ∼30 each generation.
source: Given that the sex-averaged number of COs is ∼30 each generation (e.g., [Fledel-Alon et al., 2011]), the number of NCOs that we detect is thus in rough agreement with a 10:1 NCO to CO ratio genome-wide (Baudat and de Massy, 2007; Cole et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: The number of NCOs detected is in rough agreement with a 10:1 NCO to CO ratio genome-wide.
source: Given that the sex-averaged number of COs is ∼30 each generation (e.g., [Fledel-Alon et al., 2011]), the number of NCOs that we detect is thus in rough agreement with a 10:1 NCO to CO ratio genome-wide (Baudat and de Massy, 2007; Cole et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous estimates.

claim: Assuming heterozygosity rate π = 10−3, roughly 17 (95% CI 13–21) variable sites are expected to experience NCO in each meiosis.
source: Assuming that the heterozygosity rate is π = 10−3 (The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2012), roughly 17 (95% CI 13–21) variable sites are expected to experience NCO in each meiosis.
evidence: This is calculated from the NCO rate and heterozygosity.

claim: The estimate of variable sites experiencing NCO is on the same order as the number of sites affected by de novo mutation in each generation.
source: This estimate is on the same order as the number of sites affected by de novo mutation in each generation (Ségurel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with mutation rates from a previous study.

claim: The observed GC transmission rate of 68% (95% CI 59–78%) provides a direct confirmation of the presence of gBGC.
source: More generally, our results provide a direct confirmation of the presence of gBGC, and lend strong support to the hypothesis that it could play a major role in shaping base composition over evolutionary timescales (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the GC transmission data.

claim: The results lend strong support to the hypothesis that gBGC could play a major role in shaping base composition over evolutionary timescales.
source: More generally, our results provide a direct confirmation of the presence of gBGC, and lend strong support to the hypothesis that it could play a major role in shaping base composition over evolutionary timescales (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the GC transmission data.

claim: The estimated rate of GC transmission (68%) is high relative to what was found in the recent sperm-typing study, where only two of six hotspots had such a bias (∼70%).
source: Our estimated rate of GC transmission is high relative to what was found in the recent sperm-typing study, where only two of six hotspots had such a bias (∼70%) (Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study.

claim: Under certain conditions on mutation, the ascertainment bias of SNP genotyping arrays could lead SNPs subject to stronger biased gene conversion to be enriched, leading to slight over-estimation of the strength of biased gene conversion across the genome.
source: In that regard, one possible caveat is that, under certain conditions on mutation, the ascertainment bias of SNP genotyping arrays could lead SNPs subject to stronger biased gene conversion to be enriched, and thus lead us to slightly over-estimate the strength of biased gene conversion across the genome.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential bias.

claim: A recent reanalysis of data from S. cerevisiae showed that gBGC is associated with CO gene conversions but not NCOs, with a GC transmission rate of ≤55%.
source: Interestingly, a recent reanalysis of data from S. cerevisiae (Mancera et al., 2008) showed that in this species of yeast, gBGC is associated with CO gene conversions but not NCOs, with a GC transmission rate of ≤55% (Lesecque et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study in yeast.

claim: In humans, gBGC does operate in NCO events, pointing to a difference in repair mechanisms between humans and yeast.
source: Both our findings and recent results from human sperm (Odenthal-Hesse et al., 2014) indicate that in contrast, in humans, gBGC does operate in NCO events, pointing to a difference in repair mechanisms between humans and yeast that remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing human and yeast data.

claim: NCO tract lengths vary over more than an order of magnitude, from hundreds to thousands of base pairs.
source: Considering the distribution of SNPs in NCO tracts, we found lengths that vary over more than an order of magnitude, from hundreds to thousands of base pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the tract length data.

claim: A study of de novo mutations reported observing regions with NCO sites across intervals spanning between 2–11 kb.
source: As a potential example of the same phenomenon, a study of de novo mutations reported observing regions with NCO sites across intervals spanning between 2–11 kb (Campbell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: The complex NCO resolutions may arise through patchy GC biased repair across long stretches of heteroduplex DNA or repeated template switching during the repair of DSBs.
source: In any case, the complex NCO resolutions seen in our pedigree data has not been reported in mammals previously, and is consistent with either with patchy GC biased repair across long stretches of heteroduplex DNA or repeated template switching during the repair of DSBs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The complex NCO events may arise through mitotic recombination, a process that has been found to produce similar patterns in yeast.
source: Alternatively, these events may arise through mitotic recombination, a process that has been found to produce similar patterns in yeast (St Charles and Petes, 2013; Yin and Petes, 2013).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation citing findings from yeast.

claim: Understanding the source of complex NCO events will be important for studies of mammalian recombination and for improving population genetic models of haplotypes and LD.
source: Understanding their source will be important for studies of mammalian recombination and for improving population genetic models of haplotypes and LD.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of future research.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of human pedigrees will enable unbiased analyses of de novo NCO at relatively high resolution.
source: Going forward, whole genome sequencing of human pedigrees will enable unbiased analyses of de novo NCO at relatively high resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.
